﻿Process Electrification


*    Electrification of Coal/Gas-Based On Process Heating
Process heating electrification means replacing a process heater that currently burns coal, natural gas, furnace oil, or another fuel with an electric heating technology. It is especially relevant for industrial processes that require direct or indirect heat.    




   
Field
	Value
	Process
	Replaces coal/gas combustion used for process heating with electric resistance heating, induction heating, infrared heating, microwave heating, electric furnaces, or other electric technologies.
	Temperature
	Depends on the technology and process. Electric systems can provide anything from low-temperature heating (<150°C) to very high temperatures above 1,000°C for suitable industrial applications.
	Energy source
	Electricity, ideally supplied from renewable sources such as solar or wind for maximum emissions reduction.
	Efficiency
	Electric heating can achieve approximately 80–99% point-of-use efficiency, depending on the technology and process. There are no direct combustion/flue-gas losses at the heating point.
	CAPEX
	Highly variable. Simple electric heaters may require relatively low investment, while industrial electric furnaces, induction systems, high-power transformers and electrical infrastructure can require substantial CAPEX.
	OPEX
	Depends strongly on electricity and fuel prices. Electricity-based heating can have higher energy costs in some locations, but savings can come from higher efficiency, reduced fuel handling and lower maintenance.
	Lifetime
	Typically 10–20+ years, depending on the heating technology, operating temperature, duty cycle and maintenance. Heating elements may need periodic replacement.
	Space
	Often smaller than equivalent combustion systems, because burners, fuel storage, fuel-preparation systems and large exhaust systems can be eliminated.
	Constraints
	Requires sufficient electrical capacity, suitable electric-heating technology for the required temperature/process, reliable electricity supply, and potentially expensive electrical upgrades. Electricity tariffs can significantly affect economics.
	                                                                                        
* Boiler Electrification
Boiler electrification means replacing a conventional coal, diesel, LPG, furnace-oil or gas-fired boiler with an electric boiler or another electric steam-generation system. Instead of burning fuel to produce steam, the system uses electricity to heat water and generate steam.
Field
	Value
	Process
	Steam generation for dyeing, drying, sterilizing, cooking, washing, chemical processing and other industrial processes
	Temperature
	Steam/process heat typically ~100–350°C, depending on steam pressure and boiler design
	Energy source
	Grid electricity; can also be supplied partly by renewable electricity such as solar PV
	Efficiency
	Typically ~95–99% at the point of use
	CAPEX
	Roughly ₹4–5 lakh for small 100–500 kW systems → ₹25–65 lakh for 500 kW–1 MW → ₹65 lakh–₹1.6 crore+ for 1–5 MW systems, depending on pressure, capacity and installation
	OPEX
	Medium–High — mainly electricity cost; strongly dependent on Indian electricity tariff and operating hours
	Lifetime
	Typically ~20–25 years, with proper maintenance
	Space
	Compact — no fuel yard or chimney required
	Constraints
	High electricity demand, grid capacity, electricity tariff, 3-phase supply, power reliability and possible electrical-infrastructure upgrades
	Additional important points:
Field
	Value
	Existing equipment it can replace/reduce
	Coal, diesel, LPG, furnace-oil or gas-fired boilers
	Maintenance required
	Boiler inspection, water treatment, electrical-system inspection, heating-element/electrode maintenance and pump/valve maintenance
	Backup required?
	Recommended for continuous industrial production; existing fuel boiler can be retained as backup
	Thermal storage
	Optional; can be combined with hot-water/steam thermal storage to shift electricity use
	Emissions reduction
	Eliminates direct combustion emissions at the factory; total CO₂ reduction depends on the electricity source
	Best suited for
	Indian MSMEs with reliable grid electricity, especially textile, food, dairy, pharmaceutical, chemical and other steam-intensive industries
	Boiler electrification is the replacement of a fossil-fuel-fired boiler with an electric boiler that uses electricity instead of burning coal, diesel, LPG or gas to generate steam. It can eliminate on-site combustion, reduce local air pollution and provide highly controllable steam, but its operating cost depends strongly on electricity tariffs and available grid capacity.
MSME optimizer
The basic flow is:
Grid electricity → Electric boiler → Steam → Industrial process
For example:
Coal/Gas boiler ❌ → Electric boiler ✅ → Steam → Textile dyeing
Important: Boiler electrification is most attractive when the MSME has adequate electrical capacity, reasonable electricity tariffs and a need to eliminate fossil-fuel combustion. The optimizer should compare the existing boiler's fuel cost + efficiency + emissions against the electric boiler's electricity consumption + tariff + electrical upgrade cost.
* Dryer Electrification
Dryer electrification means replacing a coal, diesel, LPG, furnace-oil or gas-fired dryer with an electrically powered drying system. Electricity can produce hot air or heat directly, which removes moisture from products without fuel combustion.
Field
	Value
	Process
	Drying of food, textiles, chemicals, paper, wood, agricultural products, pharmaceuticals and other industrial materials
	Temperature
	Typically ~50–250°C for many industrial dryers; depends on product and dryer design
	Energy source
	Grid electricity; can also use electricity from solar PV
	Efficiency
	Typically ~70–95%, depending on dryer type, insulation, airflow and moisture-removal requirements
	CAPEX
	Roughly ₹3–10 lakh for small MSME dryers → ₹10–50 lakh+ for medium industrial systems, depending on capacity, temperature and dryer type
	OPEX
	Medium–High — mainly electricity cost; depends strongly on electricity tariff and operating hours
	Lifetime
	Typically ~10–20 years, depending on dryer type, operating temperature and maintenance
	Space
	Moderate — depends on dryer capacity and configuration
	Constraints
	Electricity availability, electricity tariff, drying temperature, moisture content, airflow, product sensitivity and required drying time
	Additional important points:
Field
	Value
	Existing equipment it can replace/reduce
	Gas, LPG, diesel, coal or furnace-oil-fired dryers and hot-air generators
	Maintenance required
	Heating-element inspection, fan/blower maintenance, temperature-controller checks, cleaning and insulation inspection
	Backup required?
	Recommended for continuous production where grid reliability is poor; existing fuel-fired dryer can be retained as backup
	Thermal storage
	Optional; can be combined with thermal storage when heat needs to be shifted to different operating periods
	Emissions reduction
	Eliminates direct combustion emissions at the dryer; total CO₂ reduction depends on the electricity source
	Best suited for
	Indian MSMEs in food processing, textile, pharmaceutical, chemical, paper, agricultural processing and other industries requiring controlled drying
	In the same simple style:
Dryer electrification is the replacement of a fossil-fuel-fired industrial dryer with an electrically powered dryer. Instead of burning coal, diesel, LPG or gas to produce hot air, electricity is used to generate and control the required heat for removing moisture from products. It can reduce on-site air pollution and provide precise temperature control, but operating cost depends strongly on electricity tariffs.
MSME optimizer
The basic flow is:
Grid electricity → Electric heating system → Hot air/heat → Wet product → Dry product
For example:
LPG dryer ❌ → Electric dryer ✅ → Hot air → Textile/Food drying
For  optimizer: select the dryer based on required drying temperature, moisture removal, product type, operating hours, electricity tariff and available electrical capacity.
